Based on the two transcript files, here are the 10 most extreme, conspiratorial, or factually unhinged claims made during the Sarah Westall / Michael Letts interview:

1. "Military tribunals have been initiated and indictments are forthcoming" Letts claims military tribunals have been "created" and "charged," with indictments ready to be served against high-profile figures including Obama, Brennan, and Susan Rice. He presents this as an ongoing, real operation — while admitting the public won't see them until "the investigation is complete." This is a years-old conspiracy theory that has never materialized.
2. "68–70% of the deficit is caused by embezzlement, fraud, and stealing — almost 100% with interest" Letts asserts that internal documents show most of the national deficit is due to stolen money, and that when you add interest on the stolen money, it approaches 100% of the deficit. He provides no source, no document, and no verification. This is an extraordinary claim presented as fact.
3. "We have two options: military tribunals or another revolution" Letts frames the choice as either military tribunals or a 1776-style revolution — explicitly invoking the possibility of mass destruction and comparing it to dropping the atomic bomb in WWII. This is rhetoric that normalizes the overthrow of the civilian government.
4. "Congress is a mafia bigger than the mob ever was" Letts claims the corruption is a global criminal organization "headquartered" in the US, controlling the world's most powerful military and wealthiest country. He says it's the "most elaborate, most sophisticated criminal organization ever to exist in history." This is hyperbolic conspiracy framing.

5. "FEMA didn't have money for North Carolina flood victims because it was transferred to illegals — and that's why they didn't care" This is a distorted claim. Letts says FEMA's budget was moved to help illegal immigrants, which is why flood victims got no help. The reality is more nuanced (FEMA disaster relief funding is separate from other programs), but it's presented as proof of deliberate malice.
6. "They're stealing your tax money through NGOs, and Congress members sit on the boards" Letts claims Congress creates thousands of NGOs to funnel government money, and that members of Congress serve on these boards and get paid substantial sums without even attending meetings. This is presented as the mechanism of theft — but no specific evidence is offered.
7. "They're propping up Andrew Tate and Pearl Davis to accelerate moral decay" Westall claims she ran a "vocal print" analysis showing that figures like Andrew Tate and Pearl Davis are being propped up by the same forces to "help the moral decay quicken" and give people hopelessness. This is a conspiracy theory about influencer culture.
8. "The Christian base is being controlled by twisting scripture to destroy women" Westall and Letts claim that there's a deliberate effort to use Christianity to attack women — telling them they need to be subservient and shouldn't vote — as part of a broader strategy to defang and control the Christian base. Letts, an ordained Baptist minister, validates this.

9. "The justice system is a kangaroo court — judges ignore the Supreme Court" Letts claims activist judges simply "give a finger to the Supreme Court" and change a word or two in their rulings to defy them. He says the US has a "third world country kind of thing" because judges don't follow the rule of law. This is a sweeping indictment of the entire judiciary.
10. "We're in a PSY-OP war — they're so good at making it look like they care" Both speakers repeatedly frame everything as a "psychological operation" and "psy-op war," claiming the media, tech companies, and influencers are all part of a coordinated effort to manipulate the public. This framing allows any contradictory evidence to be dismissed as part of the psy-op.
A note on the broader pattern:
Nearly every claim in this conversation is unfalsifiable —

indictments are "coming," operations are "unrevealed for national security," and evidence is always just around the corner. The conversation mixes legitimate frustrations about government corruption with extreme conspiracy theories, calls for military tribunals, and revolutionary rhetoric. It's a textbook example of how real issues can be hijacked by conspiratorial thinking that offers no verifiable path forward.

text:
MAN ARRESTED AFTER BLOCKING A HIKING TRAIL IN A GORILLA SUIT AND CHARGING BANANA TOLLS

ASHEVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA — Wyatt Prescott, 54, blocked a trail in a gorilla suit and told hikers they owed him bananas or cash. The payment arrangement became contentious when one visitor offered a slightly bruised apple.

His sign offered a discount for groups and said exact change was preferred, despite the advertised currency being bananas. Several hikers thought it was a charity event until he refused to identify a charity. He called it habitat maintenance. A walker asked whether they could simply pass on the other side. He moved over and described that route as the express lane. The costume made it difficult to hear his explanations, which did not improve the terms when he repeated them.

The toll booth consisted of a folding chair placed across a public trail and a hand-lettered sign with surprisingly firm payment terms. Hikers without bananas were offered a cash alternative. One asked whether the money went toward trail maintenance. He said keeping the trail exclusive was maintenance. Behind him, a queue formed that included two dogs, a family with snacks, and a visitor who had already called for help.

Rangers found a queue forming behind his improvised checkpoint. He described himself as an immersive attraction, although nobody had purchased an attraction ticket.

He was arrested after refusing to clear the path. A hiker asked whether the experience came with parking validation.

Post-October 7, 2023; Palestinian cinema produced an urgent, hybrid body of work documenting catastrophe in real time while referencing the Nakba as an unfinished event.  

Together they form a distinctive cinema of "witnessing": formally inventive, produced under extreme constraint, and increasingly visible on the international festival and awards circuit.  And recently, their Palestinian / Arab creators are joined by sympathetic Israeli filmmakers.

Recurring themes include "sumud" (steadfastness), the ordinary made extraordinary by contextual violence (finding milk, teaching children, making art), family as both refuge and site of inherited wound, the journalist or artist as both witness and target, and the land itself as character.  Children and young victims recur as moral centers.  Historical context grounds these works in relation to the Nakba, not as deep background but as active present: displacement, house demolitions, and intergenerational memory pervade and compel the narratives.  

Stylistically the works are hybrids.  Perhaps most harrowingly, The Voice of Hind Rajab grafts real audio onto a real-time thriller.  The early anthology From Ground Zero mixes genres and phone footage while the most recent NAZA uses obscured faces and nighttime rooftops for testimony.  As historical films intercut archival material, the cumulative result is a consistent body of cinematic work that refuses polished distance: sound design often foregrounds drones, explosions, or crackling phone lines; while visual style ranges from intimate video-call frames to reconstructed period villages.

This is not “war cinema" but a cinema of both the unimaginable and the unfilmable made under conditions that would normally halt production.  Its distinctiveness lies in the combination of formal experimentation (hybrid docudrama, anthology as collective testimony), ethical risk (using a child’s real dying voice, anonymized perpetrators speaking casually of mass death), and historical layering that treats October 2023 as one more chapter in a 76-year catastrophe.  While festival reception - record ovations, prizes, Oscar shortlists - has given it unusual visibility, distribution / exhibition in some markets remains limited and even contested.  As an archival collective, the works insist that the people living through the events, not only those observing from outside, will / should shape how they are remembered and depicted.

Where earlier Palestinian cinema humanized the Palestinian people against stereotypes of victim or militant, the post-Oct. 7th new wave documents the progressive erasure of the conditions that made those earlier stories possible.  Continuity exists in the commitment to sumud and self-representation; the triggering rupture is in scale, urgency, and the sense that the camera itself is now a form of survival.
___________________________
SELECTED FILMOGRAPHY

From Ground Zero (2024)

An anthology of 22 shorts (documentary, fiction, animation, experimental) by Gazan directors, produced by Masharawi.  Shot in late 2023 under bombardment, it premiered in Amman and Toronto, and later became Palestine’s 2025 Oscar entry.  Critics praised its “cumulative emotional impact” and mosaic of survival, humor, and art-making amid destruction; some found it uneven. 

FULL MOVIE: Palestinian Movie - From Ground Zero - (Subs: English, Português, Türkçe) https://t.co/4yIAYNoO7l via @YouTube

Palestine 36 (2025) 

Annemarie Jacir’s historical epic on the 1936–39 Arab Revolt against British rule.  Production began in the West Bank, moved to Jordan, and returned for final scenes.  It features Hiam Abbass, Saleh Bakri, Jeremy Irons, and Liam Cunningham, plus archival footage.  When submitted as Palestine’s Oscar submission, it received strong reviews as a “stirring,” “sweeping” primer that draws explicit parallels to the present. 

The story unfolds in 1936 as a general strike and armed uprising erupt against British colonial policies, land sales, and rising Jewish immigration after the Balfour Declaration.  It interweaves multiple perspectives rather than following a single protagonist.  The film opens with a train arriving in Jerusalem and moves between village fields, Jerusalem streets, Jaffa docks, and British administrative spaces, incorporating colorized archival footage. The narrative builds toward British reprisals against villages, the Peel Commission partition proposal, and a devastating assault on Al Basma.  

Significantly, director Jacir described it as showing that “our history does not begin with the Nakba.”  Principal photography was scheduled to start 14 October 2023 in Palestine (West Bank, Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Jaffa) but was halted after 7 October.  The production relocated to Jordan for much of the shoot, then returned to Palestine in late 2024 with a reduced crew to complete key scenes, making it the only feature filmed in Palestine during the first two years of the Gaza bombing.   Jacir insisted on finishing the film in Palestine rather than making “another refugee film.” 

All That’s Left of You (2025) 

Cherien Dabis’s multi-generational drama spanning 1948 Nakba Jaffa through the First Intifada to the 2020s.  Relocated from the West Bank to Cyprus / Jordan / Greece.  This film was Jordan’s Oscar entry.  It traces inherited trauma across one family. 

Palestine 36 and All That’s Left of You explicitly treat the 1936 revolt and 1948 Nakba as origins of the present catastrophe.  Earlier films such as Farha (2021) continue to circulate in commemorative programs as retrospectives and Nakba-focused works proliferate.  Indeed, the ongoing discourse surrounding "genocide" and "ethnic cleansing" has made the “continuing Nakba” theme a central framing rather than a distant historical event.

The Voice of Hind Rajab (2025)

Written and directed by Tunisian filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania: an 89-minute docudrama set almost entirely inside a Palestine Red Crescent call center in Ramallah.  It reconstructs the hours on 29 January 2024 when five-year-old Hind Rajab, trapped in a bullet-riddled car in Gaza City amid the bodies of relatives, pleaded for rescue.  The film uses the actual audio recordings of Hind’s calls while actors (Motaz Malhees as operator Omar, Saja Kilani as supervisor Rana, Clara Khoury, Amer Hlehel) play the responders.

Production was a Tunisia-France co-production (Tanit Films, Mime Films, JW Films, RaeFilm Studios); principal photography took place in Tunisia.  Hollywood figures including Brad Pitt, Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, Alfonso Cuarón, and Jonathan Glazer later joined as executive producers.  It premiered in competition at Venice 2025, won the Grand Jury Prize plus six parallel awards, received a reported 23-minute standing ovation, became Tunisia’s Oscar submission, and earned Golden Globe and Academy Award nominations for Best International Feature. 

Critics have called it “harrowing,” “fierce, urgent and heart-shattering,” and “a powerful appeal to humanity.”  The Guardian noted its “startling audacity” in mixing real audio with dramatized tension.  Sight & Sound praised its emotional devastation while questioning whether embedding a dead child’s real voice inside a genre-inflected narrative “blurs the boundary between resistance and spectacle.”  Ben Hania has said she made it “to bear witness and not feel helpless,” arguing cinema’s task is “provoking empathy” rather than further explanation. 

Citizen Osama (2026)

Directed by Gazan filmmaker Ahmed Hassouna: a 69-minute documentary following journalist and photographer Osama Al-Ashi through his first year of fatherhood amid the war.  Hassouna (who previously contributed to the From Ground Zero anthology) shoots Al-Ashi documenting rubble, searching for baby formula and diapers, navigating bombed streets, and mourning colleagues such as Al-Jazeera’s Ismail al-Ghoul.  It is a Palestine-France co-production associated with Rashid Masharawi and Laura Nikolov’s Gaza-focused initiative. 

The film premiered out of competition at Venice 2026 and was selected as Palestine’s official Oscar submission for 2027.   Because the director remains in Gaza and could not attend Venice, the film itself becomes part of the story of blocked movement and targeted journalists.  Reviews describe it as “an extraordinary portrait of the struggle to live in Gaza” that “underlines the incredible resilience of the Palestinian people” while showing the journalist himself as a civilian under the same bombardment. Some critics noted it offers intimate glimpses but limited broader context. 

NAZA (2026)

Directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (the Israeli half of the Oscar-winning No Other Land team), is a British production (The Guardian, JW Films, with Jonathan Glazer as executive producer).  Shot secretly on Tel Aviv rooftops over three years, it consists of anonymized nighttime interviews with 24 Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers who describe targeting systems that treated expected civilian deaths - “NAZA,” a military acronym for collateral damage - as an accepted variable. 

Officers recount AI-assisted strikes on homes, “daddy’s home” signals from children’s phones triggering attacks, and accepted ratios that reached hundreds of civilians per target.  It premiered in Venice competition in September 2026 and won the Special Jury Prize.  Reviews have called it “a bombshell,” “one of the most important films of our time,” and a “devastating exposé” that drew comparison to Shoah.

Variety called it “a more devastating exposé of Israeli genocidal policy” than No Other Land.  Vulture described it as “one of the most important films of our time… a bombshell" while the Hollywood Reporter praised its “outrage… contempt… on a profound level.”  While some Israeli and pro-Israel outlets dismissed it as one-sided or Holocaust-analogizing, co-directors Abraham and Szor framed it as an obligation to examine “the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible.”

Harvesting Grace, A Forty-Day Devotional by C.S. McDonald is a warm, reflective Christian devotional that invites readers to slow down and reconnect with God’s grace, especially during the beauty of autumn.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. Each entry includes a daily Bible verse, a peaceful and thought-provoking observation, and soft reflections designed to refresh faith and cultivate joy. McDonald encourages readers to pause amid life’s busyness, sit quietly or take a walk, and intentionally harvest God’s steadfast love and boundless grace. It serves as a humble, encouraging guide that can be used in autumn or anytime throughout the year. Readers looking for a calming, faith-centered companion will find it uplifting and accessible.

Buy links
- Amazon (Kindle ebook): [https://t.co/T3ipW1VfVZ](https://t.co/T3ipW1VfVZ)
- Also check Amazon and other retailers for paperback or additional formats as they become available.

About the author
C.S. McDonald taught dance and choreographed shows for twenty-six years before turning to writing. She lives with her husband Bill and their dogs on a Thoroughbred farm near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. She is the author of the popular clean Fiona Quinn Mysteries (cozy mysteries featuring a kindergarten teacher turned sleuth) and the Owl’s Nest Mysteries, as well as children’s books inspired by farm life. In recent years she has added devotionals, including *Harvesting Grace*, as part of her spiritual writing. She is a wife, mom, grandma, dog lover, and self-described helpless chocoholic.

text:
Podcast Summary | Matt and Shane's Secret Podcast: Ep 635 - Podcaster's Union (feat. Kevin Ryan & H. Foley)

Overview
Boundaries, money, and the cost of getting what you want run through this episode. The hosts and guests trade stories about failing to set limits, being put on spending restrictions, and relearning discipline through comedy, recovery, and construction work. The throughline: success rarely fixes self-control, and the systems that impose limits, from unions to credit card freezes to recovery meetings, shape behavior more than willpower does. Humor keeps the stakes bearable while the underlying tensions, trust, addiction, and class, stay visible.

Key Themes
- Boundaries are treated as aspirational: multiple speakers admit they either never set them or take them back immediately, then stew instead of acting.
- A corporate credit card dispute becomes the episode's central case study in consequences: overspending leads to access being revoked, framed as a needed reassessment rather than punishment.
- Financial asymmetry is explicit: more was spent in one 30-day stretch than a speaker earned in 2019, and trust is described as one-sided.
- Recovery is framed as transferable, not solved: GLP-1 weight loss removes a food addiction while other addictive patterns can resurface elsewhere.
- Union labor is presented as a genuine tradeoff, strong pay and protections against high employer costs, heavy drinking, long breaks, and early Fridays.
- The early Raven comedy scene is remembered as varsity-level and cutthroat, a standard whose abandonment coincided with decline.
- Construction work is remembered as formative and physically punishing, and the office world that followed felt more regimented and less honest.
- Pimping and OnlyFans are compared as business models that mix transaction with psychological control.
- Housing costs around suburban Philadelphia are cited as roughly a million dollars for ordinary houses, feeding generational anxiety about whether hard work still buys stability.

Detailed Summary
The episode opens on boundaries, and almost nobody claims competence. One speaker says he has never successfully drawn a line and routinely takes it back the moment he does. Another says he lets people cross his boundaries and then stews about it privately. The quiet flight gets joked about as the closest thing to enforcement anyone manages.

Fame and its discomforts get probed through a specific airport story. One speaker was recognized by someone named Colin while carrying an audition script in his back pocket and wearing sunglasses. He had checked a bag and was flying to Cleveland to see a woman, with an audition coming up. The script was sides for the role, and he later turned the part down because he did not like it. He also mentions auditioning because a producer was loosely related to his family, joking about nepotism. Tulsa King and Land Man come up in that context.

Network television edits of Yellowstone get criticized as ruining the show. A money tree enters the conversation, with one speaker saying he kept one for roughly seven years and that his ex-wife now has it. A thermostat set to 70 degrees gets mocked. A plant whose name the owner does not know gets called a monster.

The credit card conflict is the episode's structural backbone. Charges built up over a couple of weeks, access was taken away, and one speaker jokes about writing it off as a tax deduction. The card was American Express. A specific dispute centers on flights: one person says he never put a flight on the card, the other says six flights were charged, and the first then admits he used the wrong card. The consequence, a badge or gun being taken away, is described as acceptable. The incident is referred to as the Karen situation with the AMX.

The relationship framing underneath the money story is blunt. One person is described as the only person in the speaker's life he does not question, while also being someone who put him through hell over the past year. The spending was extreme: more was spent in a recent 30-day period than the speaker made in 2019. The restriction is framed as a reassessment rather than malice. The group, marriage, and creative partnership are described as recovering and doing well, with the podcast at its biggest and a special coming out.

Comedy origin stories fill in the apprenticeship. First-half Raven sets were remembered as varsity level, and bombing there sent you back to the second half. McKver and Pope are remembered as comedians who seemed far ahead and locked in. One speaker was asked to close as a young comic, wrote a new five minutes, and visibly lost the room after roughly 45 seconds. Tommy gets credit for a pre-set pointer: big smile before going on stage. A Philly's Funniest story follows the same pattern, making the finals on a first competition, doing all new material, and bombing.

Recovery and addiction get serious treatment. One speaker states his last relapse was March 6, and he attends meetings and therapy. Weight loss is stated at 100 to 120 pounds, from a starting weight of 435. He describes a food addiction and having attended sex and love addict meetings. The conversation draws a comparison to claims about Subway's Jared Fogle, and to GLP-1 drugs like Zepbound potentially causing relapse into other addictions. The working theory: the substance or behavior changes, the underlying pattern does not.

OnlyFans enters as a modern riff on pimping economics. Content creators record a year of content then stop, while teams manage messages for what is described as banking revenue. Pimping itself is described as combining business transaction with courtship and psychological control, not purely transactional. Bishop Don Juan and Old School are referenced.

Union labor gets a long segment framed as a tradeoff rather than a verdict. Union construction offers strong pay and benefits, but can also involve heavy drinking, long breaks, and early Friday finishes. Union laborers sweeping up can earn around 500 dollars a day, while union plumbers and pipe fitters can cost employers 200 thousand dollars or more per year in pay, benefits, and dues. Electricians are described working 7 to 9, taking a 30-minute coffee break, a three-hour lunch, then wrapping early on Fridays. A family saying captures the attitude: if it ain't done by noon on Friday, it ain't happening.

Some workers use union jobs as a stepping stone to start their own non-union companies. A coffee shop in Philly reportedly shut down all locations after baristas threatened to unionize, and Walmart allegedly had a rapid-response union-busting team flying in on a private jet. Roughly eight cities still have trade unions, including Chicago and Philadelphia. Union business agents reportedly demand additional union workers on non-union jobs, with one story involving a father challenging an agent to a parking lot fight. Historical tactics allegedly included cutting hydraulic lines, breaking equipment, and driving cars through storefronts. The inflatable rat gets its mention as the recognizable symbol.

Construction stories turn into a tribute to physical danger as comedy. Someone tried to cut copper bus bars out of a live industrial electrical panel and was launched across the basement, cutting power for the whole building. An electrician demo story involves cutting an MC wire with insulated snips, hitting the neutral, and seeing a blue arc; the foreman dismissed it as leftover electricity. Cutting the wire caused a boom, blew a hole in the metal, threw the snips, and knocked out power to a plastic surgeon's office mid-procedure, after which the surgeon said nothing happened.

Working with non-electricians who assume power is dead gets a joke about handing boots to a wife before cutting. Fathers as bosses set the tone: read the blueprint, and I am not paying you to think. Tasks included fetching channel locks, 718s, and a wonky deuce from the truck, and climbing ladders across a warehouse roof. A two-man crew setting units with a crane turns into hand signals compared to closing the World Series. The diet on site was six hot dogs at 11:00, cheese and pizza lunches, ice cream on the way home, and a father who developed severe type 2 diabetes.

The first office job after college brought culture shock. A crude weekend recap got shut down by a female boss, and the law firm job paid 12 dollars an hour entry-level accounting. Clocking out felt regimented: employees were forced to sit until 5:00 instead of lining up at 4:59. Overnight supermarket work involved cutting floors, digging, exposing mains, tying in, and dealing with night-crew toilets flushing into the hole. Snow shoveling paid emergency rates around 20 dollars an hour cash, with beers dropped in the snow and drinking and smoking while clearing condominium complexes.

Leaving the family business was driven by constant fighting with a brother and a business that was tanking. A recurring generational motivation surfaces: fathers told their sons to work indoors and in air conditioning, and the speakers relate to that advice. Housing prices around suburban Philadelphia are described as roughly a million dollars for ordinary-ish houses, with 600 thousand once seeming like a mansion. One speaker says he has spent every dollar he has ever made, framed as 100 percent efficiency. Baby boomers leaving a housing surplus as population declines gets floated, though others are skeptical and admit they cannot wrap their heads around macro issues. Budgeting is mentioned as a source of pride.

The closing stretch is banter about duvets versus comforters. One speaker distrusts prior information and insists on verifying the blanket setup, and the group distinguishes a duvet from a bed skirt or ruffle, with one admitting he misunderstood the term until around age 34. A regular down comforter by itself is considered best, with a claim that it keeps you cool. Parents are in town staying in the guest room during the blanket situation, and the task is described as fitting one blanket inside another.

Promotions close things out. The specials are titled American Garbage, with a live premiere announced for Sunday night on their YouTube channel. The podcast Are You Your Garbage is mentioned as having had Shane twice and the guest twice. New episodes of Matt and Shane Secret Podcast are promoted on Spotify. The group jokes about linking things on YouTube without resolving how, about having producers handle logistics, and about splitting a QP later and showing up in three cars ten minutes late.

Wright’s evaluation starts with command.

She produced approximately 17.9 PPG as a sophomore while shooting 43.7% from the field and 36.1% from three, earning Class 3A first-team all-state recognition, WAMAC East Player of the Year and all-tournament captain honors.

But her value extends beyond production.

Wright consistently demonstrates the qualities of an excellent floor general: she controls tempo, organizes possessions, creates advantages and understands when the game requires scoring versus distribution.

• Three-level scoring potential
• Manipulates defenders before attacking

Her 36.1% three-point shooting provides an important scalability signal. Five made threes in the state semifinal demonstrated the ability to punish defenses when coverage moves underneath actions.

2. PROCESSING + FLOOR GENERALSHIP

This may be Wright’s defining offensive trait.

She processes the floor early, controls possession tempo and consistently demonstrates an understanding of where the next advantage should come from. She is not simply a scorer playing point guard. She shows legitimate lead-guard instincts.

Wright projects as an elite point-of-attack defender and currently grades as a Top-5 POA defensive prospect nationally within OWU’s 2028 evaluation framework.

Her pressure, anticipation, lateral competitiveness and willingness to disrupt the ball can change possessions before the offense reaches its intended action. Six steals in a regional final provide production evidence behind the film signal.

At 5’5”, Wright must consistently win through skill, processing, toughness and defensive leverage.

MOKAN’s Nike Girls EYBL environment becomes critical evidence.

Wright is an OWU 3-Star prospect: a legitimate mid-major Division I recruit with a Power Four ceiling.

Ahmad Ibsais on Aljazeera”

“Recent progressive wins of outspoken Israel critics in Democratic primaries have generated a lot of optimism. Abdul El-Sayed won the Dem nomination for a Senate seat in Michigan after AIPAC + its allies spent more than $54m against him in what came to be the most expensive Dem Senate primary in US history.

“In NJ, a surgeon named Adam Hamawy, who as a medical volunteer refused to leave Gaza until last member of his team could evacuate, won a 12-person primary in a House of Reps race.

“Years ago, such breakthroughs would have seemed impossible. For many on the left, it now seems like their hard work at the grassroots level is paying off.

“And yet, all the talk of a “shift on Israel” within the Dem Party is premature. The Dem establishment remains firmly in the Israeli camp, even if it is striking a more critical tone ahead of midterm elections. We should not mistake election-season displays of sympathy for a human-rights awakening on Palestine.

“We have now reached a point where the shift in attitudes towards Israel can no longer be ignored. A May poll by New York Times/Siena suggested that nearly 3/4 of Dem voters did not approve of aid for Israel. Another survey by Quinnipiac Univ showed that 66% of Dems thought US was too supportive of Israel. A poll published in April by Pew Research found that 80% of Dems viewed Israel unfavourably – up from 53% in 2022.

“These numbers have made the Dem leadership realise that open support for genocidaires is becoming too costly politically. Dem voters, who watched a livestreamed genocide, clearly no longer see Palestine as a secondary issue in their political and moral choices.
…

But enough Dem Representatives still voted with Republican majority against it. The vote was politically useful precisely because it was powerless. The 103 Dem votes in favour of cutting aid to Israel gave the party something to campaign on, while ensuring Israel still had weapons it needs to continue its brutality.

“It is a strategy that the party is likely to repeat in next Congress to secure Israeli interests while appearing to acknowledge voters’ demands.

“Furthermore, the Dem establishment has shown little interest in breaking its dependence on AIPAC. In April, the Dem National Committee rejected even a symbolic resolution condemning the lobby’s interference in Dem primaries.

“AIPAC, meanwhile, has responded to its growing toxicity by learning how to disappear. Its super PAC has routed millions thru other orgs whose funding is disclosed only after voters cast their ballots. It has also directed donors through candidate-specific portals that leave individual names, rather than AIPAC’s, in public campaign records.

“Having spent more than $100m on this midterm race, AIPAC will continue to influence Dem congressional politics to ensure it is in favour of Israeli government.
…

Rep Ro Khanna, for example, has been calling for aid cuts to Israel and an end to financing for the Iron Dome. He even went on a visit to occupied West Bank where he witnessed settler violence firsthand.

“Even then, standing before the Dem National Committee earlier this month and calling for zero aid to Israel, he led with the disclaimer that Hamas’s attack must be condemned unequivocally. He still refuses to say that Palestinians have the right to self-defence.

“Brad Lander, who won NY primary for a House seat in June and was backed by NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has described what is happening in Gaza as genocide. +yet, his criticism goes only that far. He identifies as “liberal Zionist”+has made clear he does not support BDS.

“Prominent progressives like Bernie Sanders+AOC , who are already in Congress, have also demonstrated they can only offer a partial solidarity w/Palestinian people – one that does not acknowledge their status+rights as occupied people.
…

… “We must reject every attempt by the Dem Party to pay lip service to our cause; we must continue to push for real action on Israel.”

🇸🇷 Suriname

Laws Used to Suppress Women: Indigenous and Maroon customary norms (pre-1650 to the present; women’s work concentrated in horticulture and provisioning, public political and ritual offices reserved for men, polygyny in some communities, and weak individual title when the state or companies deal with male captains) [24, 25]; English proprietary and common-law household regime in Willoughbyland (1650/51–1667; 1663 patent authorizing the proprietor to make laws; coverture transplanted from Barbados/England, subsuming a married woman’s legal identity and property in her husband; assembly limited to male landowners) [21]; Colonial slave ordinances (plakaaten, 17th century–1863, prescribing corporal punishment, dress codes, bans on assembly and literacy, and a property regime that enabled owners’ sexual use of enslaved women) [2, 19]; anti-literacy and schooling bans or restrictions for enslaved persons (17th century–1863, barring formal education for the majority-female plantation workforce) [2]; Partus sequitur ventrem / maternal-status rule under slavery (17th century–1863, children of an enslaved woman born enslaved, making women’s bodies the legal engine of labor reproduction) [2]; Poenale sanctie in indenture and related labor ordinances (Chinese contract labor from the 1850s through abolition by ordinance of 8 September 1947, in force 1 January 1948, G.B. 1947 no. 140; criminalizing contract breach and locking indentured women into lower-paid field tasks and restricted mobility) [18]; Staatstoezicht / post-emancipation apprenticeship (1863–1873, compulsory plantation labor framed as training in “family life,” channeling freed women into domestic respectability and unfree contracts) [26]; Marital authority and legal incapacity of the married woman in the Suriname Civil Code (1869–1981, denying independent contracts, litigation, and property acts without the husband’s authorization; Dutch 1838 model, abolished by Decreet C-11, not in 1957) [1, 23]; British-Dutch emigration convention and indenture practice (1870/1872, gender quota plus recruiter targeting of widows, deserted women, and other isolated women for plantation indenture) [12, 18]; Huwelijksverordening Aziaten (G.B. 1908 no. 2, drafted 1907; marriageable age 13 for “Asiatic” girls and 15 for boys) [27]; Wetboek van Strafrecht (G.B. 1911 no. 1, arts. 355–358 still in force, making abortion a crime except where practice is tolerated only to save the pregnant woman’s life; morality articles long treating sex with girls under 15 as a distinct offence) [30]; Huwelijksbesluit Mohammedanen and Huwelijksbesluit Hindoes (G.B. 1940 nos. 149–150, in force 1 January 1941; civil effects for religious marriage; girls 13 / boys 15; recognition of Islamic talak with weak protection for wives; separate regime ended when the 1973 marriage revision took effect on 23 June 2003) [1, 27, 28]; Personnel Act / Ambtenarenwet provisions (flagged into the 2010s, allowing dismissal of a female civil servant upon marriage and cutting leave credit for pregnancy) [8]; 1975 Law on Nationality (until 2014, mothers could not transmit nationality on equal terms with fathers; foreign husbands of Surinamese women treated worse than foreign wives of Surinamese men) [3]; Mining Decree 1986 and Constitution art. 41 (state ownership of land and minerals, so Indigenous and Maroon women had no secure title when male authorities or the state granted concessions) [20]; discriminatory Civil Code marriage ages (15 for girls / 17 for boys until the New Civil Code, S.B. 2024 no. 164, in force 1 May 2025, set 18 for both, still with parental consent into early adulthood) [13, 29]; paternal default in names and guardianship (children historically took the father’s surname; father as sole holder of parental power until the 2025 code) [8, 29]; inferior status of extra-marital (“natural”) children and non-recognition of concubinage (the statistically common family form left partners and children weak on inheritance and housing until limited 2025 recognition after ten years’ cohabitation) [29]; and civil-marriage definition as man–woman (same-sex marriage still excluded after the 2025 code) [29].

Date of Women's Suffrage: December 9, 1948 (universal suffrage granted under Dutch administration, confirmed at independence) [4].

Women's Literacy Rate at Newton's Time (1687): <1% (Dutch slave colony barred formal education for enslaved majority, with knowledge limited to oral traditions amid plantation exploitation) [5].

Women's Literacy Rate at Maxwell's Time (1865): ~5% (post-1863 emancipation mission schools prioritized boys/conversions, with girls accessing limited domestic/religious instruction amid ethnic and labor gaps; mission estimates) [5].

Analysis of Systemic Gender Discrimination With Persistent Inequalities: Law in Suriname did not merely “lag behind” equality. For more than three centuries it organized women’s subordination as a working system: it converted enslaved women’s bodies into a legal engine of labor supply [2], extinguished the married woman’s civil personality [1, 23], licensed the marriage of girls at thirteen [27, 28], criminalized their departure from plantations [18], denied mothers the power to transmit nationality [3], and left Indigenous and Maroon women without title when the State and companies negotiated with male captains over land and minerals [20, 24, 25]. The wreckage is not metaphorical. It is recorded in statutes, ordinances, codes, and the bodies and households those instruments produced [1, 2, 19, 23]. Before the colonial codes, Indigenous and Maroon customary orders already concentrated women’s work in horticulture and provisioning while reserving public political and ritual offices for men [24, 25]. Polygyny in some communities and collective landholding that the State later treated as a male captain’s bargaining chip meant that a woman’s labor fed the village while her individual claim to land remained legally thin whenever concessions, mining, or “development” arrived [20, 24, 25]. Custom was not a romantic alternative to the Civil Code. It was another architecture in which women produced and men represented [24, 25].

English proprietary rule in Willoughbyland (1650/51–1667) transplanted coverture from Barbados and England under a 1663 patent that authorized the proprietor to make laws and confined the assembly to male landowners [21]. A married woman did not merely “depend” on her husband. Her legal identity was absorbed into his. Property, contract, and standing in court ceased to be hers [21]. The Dutch conquest of 1667 did not restore her. It replaced one metropolitan hierarchy with another and then intensified both through slavery [2, 21].

The colonial plakaaten of the seventeenth century through 1863 prescribed corporal punishment, dress codes that marked enslaved women as property on sight, bans on assembly, and a property regime that made an owner’s sexual use of an enslaved woman a feature of ownership rather than a crime against a person [2, 19]. Anti-literacy rules barred formal education for the majority-female plantation workforce [2, 5]. Partus sequitur ventrem completed the design: the child of an enslaved woman was born enslaved [2]. The law did not need to invent a new labor force. It used women’s reproductive capacity as the statutory mechanism of reproduction. A woman’s pregnancy was not a private event. It was the colony’s method of replenishing bound labor [2]. Literacy among women at Newton’s time (1687) was under one percent; knowledge survived, when it survived, in oral tradition under a regime that treated reading as a threat [5]. By Maxwell’s time (1865), two years after formal emancipation, female literacy was still only about five percent, because mission schools after 1863 prioritized boys and conversion and offered girls a narrow curriculum of domestic and religious instruction [5]. The statute had done its work: it had kept the women who produced the colony’s wealth outside the written law that governed that wealth [2, 5].

Emancipation in 1863 did not confer freedom on the terms the word suggests. Staatstoezicht, the apprenticeship of 1863–1873, compelled plantation labor under the pretext of training in “family life” [26]. Freed women were steered into domestic respectability and unfree contracts—the legal afterlife of the plantation household [26]. Indenture then recaptured female labor by other means. Chinese contract labor from the 1850s, and later British Indian and Javanese indenture under the British–Dutch emigration convention of 1870/1872, operated with gender quotas and recruiter practices that targeted widows, deserted women, and other isolated women [12, 18]. The poenale sanctie, abolished only by ordinance of 8 September 1947 (in force 1 January 1948), criminalized contract breach [18]. A woman who left the field, refused an assignment, or tried to recover mobility could be treated as an offender [18]. Task allocation locked indentured women into lower-paid field work [12, 18]. The law did not merely exploit poverty. It manufactured a female labor pool from women who had already been stripped of male “protection” and then punished them for attempting to leave [12, 18].

The Suriname Civil Code of 1869 imported the Dutch 1838 model of marital authority and legal incapacity [1, 23]. Until Decreet C-11 of 11 March 1981—not 1957—a married woman could not independently contract, litigate, or dispose of property without her husband’s authorization [1, 23]. That is 112 years in which the independent republic’s predecessor legal order, and then the independent State itself, treated the wife as a person of diminished capacity [1, 23]. Coverture by another name. The household was a jurisdiction, and the husband was its court [1]. Universal suffrage arrived on 9 December 1948 under Dutch administration and was confirmed at independence [4], but the vote did not restore the capacity the Civil Code had taken [1, 4, 23]. A woman could help elect a legislature that still required her husband’s permission to sign a contract [1, 4, 23].

Personal-status law deepened the injury by race and religion. The Huwelijksverordening Aziaten (G.B. 1908 no. 2) set the marriageable age at thirteen for “Asiatic” girls and fifteen for boys [27]. The Huwelijksbesluit Mohammedanen and Huwelijksbesluit Hindoes (G.B. 1940 nos. 149–150, in force 1 January 1941) gave civil effects to religious marriage on the same child ages, recognized Islamic talak with weak protection for wives, and maintained a separate regime until the 1973 marriage revision took effect on 23 June 2003 [1, 27, 28]. The ordinary Civil Code itself kept discriminatory marriage ages—fifteen for girls, seventeen for boys—until the New Civil Code (S.B. 2024 no. 164) entered into force on 1 May 2025 and set eighteen for both, still requiring parental consent into early adulthood [13, 29]. These were not cultural footnotes. They were licenses to place a child’s body, labor, and fertility under a husband’s authority before she had legal adulthood [13, 27, 28, 29]. The 2018 data still showed 36 percent of women aged 20–24 first married by age 18 [8, 13]. Adolescent fertility remains about 48 births per 1,000 women aged 15–19 [11, 17]. Early marriage was the statutory pathway from girlhood into truncated schooling, obstetric risk, and lifelong economic dependence [8, 13, 29].

The Wetboek van Strafrecht (G.B. 1911 no. 1, arts. 355–358), still in force, makes abortion a crime except where practice is tolerated only to save the pregnant woman’s life [30]. Morality articles long treated sex with girls under fifteen as a distinct offence while the marriage statutes simultaneously permitted those same girls to be given in marriage [27, 30]. The contradiction is the point. The State protected a husband’s access and criminalized a woman’s exit from a pregnancy she could not legally refuse to carry [30]. Personnel rules in the Ambtenarenwet, flagged into the 2010s, allowed dismissal of a female civil servant upon marriage and cut leave credit for pregnancy [8]. Public employment—the largest formal employer—was structured to punish the female body for doing what marital law required of it [8].

Independence in 1975 did not end the nationality regime that treated women as incomplete citizens. Until 2014, the 1975 Law on Nationality denied mothers equal transmission of nationality [3]. Foreign husbands of Surinamese women were treated worse than foreign wives of Surinamese men [3]. Children of Surinamese mothers and foreign fathers were exposed to statelessness and fractured belonging because the statute located the nation’s bloodline in the father [3]. A mother could give birth on Surinamese soil and still lack the legal power to make her child fully Surinamese [3]. That is not a technical defect. It is the State declining to recognize a woman as the source of political membership [3].

For Indigenous and Maroon women the injury is territorial as well as personal. Constitution article 41 and the Mining Decree 1986 vest ownership of land and minerals in the State [20]. When male authorities or the State grant concessions, women who work the gardens, fish the creeks, and hold the household economy have no secure individual title [20, 24]. The Inter-American Court in Saramaka People v. Suriname (2007) condemned the State’s failure to recognize tribal property [20], but the gendered structure of representation—captains and officials who are men dealing with a State that owns the subsurface—continues to route dispossession through male intermediaries [20, 24, 25]. A woman can lose the forest that feeds her children without ever having been the legal counterpart in the deal [20, 24].

Family law completed the erasure of the actually existing Surinamese household. Children historically took the father’s surname [8, 29]. The father was the sole holder of parental power until the 2025 Code [8, 29]. Extra-marital—“natural”—children and partners in concubinage, the statistically common family form, stood weakly on inheritance and housing until the 2025 Code offered limited recognition after ten years’ cohabitation [29]. For generations, the law refused to see the families women actually formed and then punished those families at death, eviction, and custody [29]. Civil marriage remains defined as man–woman after the 2025 Code [29]. Same-sex partners are still outside the institution the State pretends is the only legitimate household [29].

The human cost of this legal history is measurable in flesh. The 2018 National Women’s Health Survey found that 32 percent of ever-partnered women had suffered physical and/or sexual intimate-partner violence in their lifetime and 6 percent in the prior year; 17 percent of all respondents reported having been forced into sexual intercourse by a non-partner [6]. About one in three survivors never disclosed. Most never reached police or services [6, 19]. Violence is not an unfortunate remainder of “culture.” It is what happens when law spent centuries teaching that a woman’s body was usable, her word was unauthorized, and her exit from the household was a civil or criminal problem [2, 6, 19]. Plantation rape, indenture confinement, marital incapacity, child marriage, and criminal abortion are not separate stories [2, 18, 23, 27, 30]. They are sequential chapters of the same doctrine: the female body as an instrument the legal order may allocate [2, 6, 19, 30].

Reforms exist, and they matter. Suffrage in 1948 [4]; constitutional equality at independence; Decreet C-11 in 1981 [23]; CEDAW ratification in 1993 without reservations [7]; the 2014 nationality amendment [3]; CEDAW’s 2018 concluding observations demanding repeal of the civil-service marriage-and-pregnancy penalties, action on violence, and equal pay language [8, 13]; and the New Civil Code of 1 May 2025 raising the marriage age to eighteen [29]. Female adult literacy is now about 93 percent [9]. Women hold 31.4 percent of seats in the National Assembly [10]. Female tertiary enrollment is high, though STEM participation remains around 30 percent and rural and Indigenous gaps track the old mission curriculum [5, 11]. These are real gains extracted against the grain of the codes described above [8, 11, 13].

They are not acquittal. The World Bank’s 2026 gender landscape still records women’s labor-force participation at 44.9 percent against 62.9 percent for men; female youth unemployment at 37.2 percent against 18.0 percent for young men; and laws that give women only about 71 percent of the economic rights afforded to men [11]. Maternal mortality remains about 84 per 100,000 live births [11, 17]. The Global Gender Gap Report 2025 scores Suriname at 0.738—73.8 percent parity, rank 52 of 148 [16]. The Gender Inequality Index remains in the medium range, near 0.39 [17]. OECD SIGI 2023 could not even compute a clean composite for Suriname, but the available dimensions are damning: discrimination in the family scored 62 and restricted physical integrity 58 [14]. That is the legal past speaking in the present tense [14, 15]. Occupational segregation still concentrates women in informal and care work [11, 15]. Wage gaps persist [8, 11]. Abortion remains a crime [30]. Concessions still move over untitled communal land [20]. A ten-year cohabitation rule is a late, narrow apology to women who kept households the Civil Code refused to name [29].

The record is therefore not one of incomplete modernization. It is one of law used, repeatedly and with technical precision, to suppress women—enslaved, indentured, married, Indigenous, Maroon, civil-servant, mother, girl [1, 2, 8, 18, 20, 24]. Each instrument had a date, a gazette number, and a beneficiary [1, 18, 23, 27, 30]. Each transferred capacity from women to men, from households to owners, from communities to the State [2, 20, 23]. The women who lived under those rules did not experience “gender disparity.” They experienced legal annihilation of personhood, of title, of schooling, of nationality, of reproductive autonomy, and of the right to leave [1, 2, 3, 5, 20, 30]. The statutes have been amended [3, 23, 29]. The destruction they authorized is the country’s unfinished estate [6, 8, 14, 16, 17].

text:
The clip is not a hidden exposé of illegal manufacturer kickbacks. It is a pediatrician describing a real, legal, and widely documented feature of U.S. insurance contracting: pay-for-performance bonuses that treat childhood immunization rates as one quality metric among many.

Dr. Elizabeth Mumper has said that, as an independent practitioner who declined to chase high vaccination percentages, her practice forfeited more than $400,000 in incentive payments across roughly 2007–2019. That figure is an opportunity-cost claim, not proof that doctors who vaccinate get rich. Documented programs from Blue Cross plans and similar payers have typically paid a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per provider per year, capped, and bundled with other measures such as well-child visits, developmental screens, and antibiotic stewardship. Fact-checks of viral $40,000–$80,000 “vaccine bonus” claims have repeatedly shown those numbers were extrapolated from a single 2016 Michigan program and overstated.

The economics run the opposite direction from the post’s implication. Pediatric practices often lose money or break even on vaccines due to purchase prices, refrigeration, wastage, and low administration fees, especially for Vaccines for Children doses. Some practices have stopped stocking them for that reason. Insurers still attach modest bonuses because a measles hospitalization costs tens of thousands of dollars; the incentive is actuarial risk management, the same logic used for diabetes or cancer-screening metrics.

Mumper is not a random clinician who stumbled on a spreadsheet. She is a long-time critic of the CDC schedule, a former medical director of the Autism Research Institute, a faculty member with MAPS, and a frequent speaker in Children’s Health Defense and Independent Medical Alliance circles. She has argued vaccines can trigger autism in susceptible children. She has published a small, uncontrolled retrospective claiming near-zero new autism diagnoses in her practice after she altered protocols—work that Science-Based Medicine and others have called methodologically inadequate. Her testimony has been offered in Vaccine Court cases. That background explains why she frames quality metrics as “kickbacks” and why the clip travels in MAHA networks.

The post then jumps from “doctors face financial pressure to meet a quality target” to “there is no freedom in forced medical treatments.” Those are different things. Insurers reward or withhold extra payments from *providers*. Parents can still refuse shots. School and daycare rules, not insurance bonuses, are the main source of practical pressure on families. Conflating the two turns a narrow contracting issue into a broader narrative of coercion.

The underlying tension is real: any payment model that scores physicians on population-level compliance can tilt counseling away from individualized risk-benefit discussion. That is a legitimate design critique of value-based care. It does not require treating documented, modest quality incentives as secret bribes or treating every quality metric as an assault on liberty.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Shawn Ryan Show: #338 Cardinal Burke - The New Testament

Overview
Cardinal Raymond Leo Burke presents the New Testament as historically grounded and spiritually coherent, arguing that the Resurrection is supported by multiple witnesses, the empty tomb, the transformation of Jesus's body, and the conversion of St. Paul. He rejects late dating of the Gospels, defends the reliability of oral tradition, and frames the entire biblical narrative as the fulfillment of the Old Testament through Christ. The discussion moves from manuscript evidence and apostolic martyrdom to the Eucharist, the Communion of Saints, purgatory, spiritual warfare, the rosary, and Our Lady of Guadalupe, ending with a call to live as pilgrims ready to meet the Lord.

Key Themes
- The Resurrection is presented as a historical event supported by the Gospels, the empty tomb, Christ's glorified body, and Paul's conversion.
- The apostles' transformation from fear to bold proclamation and martyrdom is cited as evidence for the Resurrection.
- Claims that the Gospels were written a century or more after Jesus are rejected based on manuscript study and earlier dating.
- The New Testament fulfills rather than abolishes the Old Testament law and prophets.
- Mary is presented as chosen from all time, preserved from sin, and uniquely participating in Christ's saving work.
- The Eucharist is claimed to be the body and blood of Christ, not merely a symbol, tied to transubstantiation.
- Purgatory and the Communion of Saints are explained as the Church glorious, suffering, and militant.
- Fear of the end times is addressed directly: those living justly have nothing to fear, since Christ comes to save all that is good.
- Spiritual warfare requires Christ's power; demons can only be fought and cast out in him.

Detailed Summary
The New Testament contains 27 books: the four Gospels, Acts of the Apostles, Pauline epistles, Catholic epistles, and Revelation. The Gospels and other accounts were handed on from people who knew Jesus and the apostles, which explains their accuracy despite being written later. Oral tradition is emphasized as reliable in that culture, where people memorized long accounts accurately before the Gospels were written down.

Differences among the Gospels, such as which healings, miracles, or parables appear, are explained by different sources rather than contradiction. Four Gospels exist; three are called synoptic because they are very similar, while John's is distinct for its more elaborate theological presentation. The Gospels are described as the most important part of the New Testament because they record the saving words and deeds of Jesus Christ. All apostles were martyrs except St. John, who took Mary into his home.

St. Paul's letters are described as a treasure of teaching, including the oldest account of the institution of the Eucharist in 1 Corinthians, with a warning that receiving unworthily brings condemnation. Paul, formerly Saul, was a Pharisee who persecuted the Church and was present at the stoning of St. Stephen. His conversion involved being thrown from his horse, the Lord's question "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?", blindness, and scales falling from his eyes after baptism.

The New Testament narrative begins in the Holy Land, in Judea and Galilee, with Nazareth, Bethlehem, the Annunciation, the Incarnation, Jesus's hidden life until age 30, and his baptism by John the Baptist. At age 12, Jesus was found in the temple conversing with the rabbis, who were astounded by his knowledge. At age 30, he read from Isaiah in the synagogue and said the prophecy was fulfilled in their midst, identifying himself as the Anointed One. John the Baptist said he must decrease and Jesus must increase, calling Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

Christ is described as having both divine and human nature: he shares unity with the Father, yet also has individual human thoughts and sufferings, always in harmony with the Father's will. His agony in the garden included sweating blood and praying that the chalice of suffering be taken away, while concluding, "not my will but thy will be done." On the cross, he cried out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" out of the greatness of his suffering, not because he believed the Father had abandoned him. His final words are described as "It is consummated," indicating completion of his work.

The crucifixion is framed as the central demonstration of God's love. Christ's suffering, death, and resurrection are meant to show that God loves humanity, created in his image, and seeks eternal union with them. Mel Gibson's film The Passion is mentioned for showing the cruelty of the Passion—flagellations, beatings, blood loss, carrying the cross, and crucifixion—rather than a sanitized version. God is said to have suffered in human nature, as shown by the crucifix.

Christ is presented as the new Adam and Mary as the new Eve: Adam failed, Christ accomplished the mission; Eve failed, Mary restores woman's dignity and place in God's plan. Mary was preserved from any stain of sin from the moment of her conception. Devotion to Mary is argued not to diminish Christ but to deepen love for him, since her life is entirely directed toward Jesus.

After his death and burial, Christ descended not into eternal punishment but into Hades, the place of the just dead, and brought them to heaven. Some sacred art depicts him leading Adam and Eve out by the hand. Purgatory is explained as a place of preparation for heaven, where souls are purified of sinfulness and temporal punishment before entering heaven. The Communion of Saints includes the Church glorious in heaven, the Church suffering in purgatory, and the Church militant on earth; the living can help the dead by prayer, and the dead can pray for the living.

Purgatory is supported from Scripture through 2 Maccabees: Jewish soldiers killed in battle were found with pagan amulets, and a collection was taken for prayers to be said for them in Jerusalem. The month of November is dedicated to the poor souls in purgatory, praying for them and honoring the dead. Indulgences can be gained through the Church for oneself and the faithful departed to hasten their arrival in heaven. Sufferings accepted and united to Christ can be offered for others, including souls in purgatory.

Opposition to Jesus began practically from the start of his public ministry, including accusations of blasphemy for forgiving sins and an attempt to throw him off a cliff. People largely opposed Jesus because they did not want a Messiah who was not an earthly ruler, not someone who made everyone rich or politically free, but one who came to save from sin and conquer evil. Jesus was 33 years old when he entered Jerusalem for his final Passover. Judas betrayed him for 30 coins, later tried to return the money, and hanged himself; the money was used to buy the Potter's Field.

The Last Supper is framed as the institution of the Eucharist and the priesthood, directly anticipating Christ's sacrifice on Calvary. The Eucharist is explicitly claimed to be the body and blood of Christ, not merely a symbol, tied to transubstantiation and the Council of Trent. The Last Supper is identified as the first Mass, placed on Holy Thursday evening, before Christ's death on Good Friday. At the Last Supper, Jesus used bread and wine to signify his body given up and blood poured out, commanding "do this in memory of me."

Jesus was arrested in the Garden of Gethsemane after Judas identified him with a kiss, then condemned by Pontius Pilate to death by crucifixion despite Pilate finding no fault in him. Pilate yielded to crowd pressure and fear of a riot, even though his wife warned him against condemning Jesus after a dream. The apostles scattered in fear during the Passion; only John remained at the cross. Jesus's side was pierced by a Roman soldier, and blood and water flowed out, presented as a sign of sacramental grace: baptism and the Eucharist, linked to devotion to the Sacred Heart.

After the Resurrection, Jesus appeared for 40 days, including to Thomas, to disciples fishing, and to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, where he was recognized in the breaking of bread. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended on the fearful apostles, transforming them into bold proclaimers; Peter preached and several thousand were baptized that day. Pentecost marks a turning point: fearful, weak disciples become bold after the Holy Spirit descends. Thousands were baptized on that day alone, beginning a continuous flow of grace as people are taught, receive faith, ask for baptism, and become members of the Church as the mystical body of Christ.

The apostles' worldwide mission and willingness to die is presented as itself a miracle; all the apostles except John were put to death. John the Apostle was not martyred, lived to a good age, is described as perhaps one of the younger apostles, especially devoted to Jesus, called his beloved disciple, and had special closeness to the Lord. The Book of Revelation is attributed to St. John the Apostle, who received visions at Patmos, where he lived with Mary. Revelation includes the vision of the Lord's coming in glory to inaugurate his wedding feast, letters to important cities and churches, and the Lord seated in glory, returning to consummate the saving work by turning all being over to the Father.

At the end, the Lord himself descends to earth in glory, in flesh and blood, but glorified. There will be a new heaven and a new earth; heaven is not simply here, but the earth will be transformed. Those alive at the final transformation will not die but will be transformed and caught up into the new creation. The gate to heaven is described as narrow because people should not presume on divine mercy, though God's mercy is also described as abundant and the saved as innumerable. Predicting the end of the world is not our concern; it belongs to God the Father, and we are to be watching and ready like good and faithful servants.

Fathers are called to sacrificial, virtuous leadership—protecting wives, modeling virtue, disciplining children, and accepting that children may resent "no" in the short term but understand it later. St. Joseph is presented as the model for men: protecting Mary and Jesus, working as a carpenter, and leading the home. Pornography is described as highly accessible to young people, especially on phones, requiring fathers to be vigilant and insist on what is good and right.

Demons can only be fought and cast out in Christ; presuming to battle Satan on one's own leads to defeat. Demonic activity is described as notably present today. Satan is described as hating humans because they are made in God's image and destined to be with God. Protection from the evil one is linked to prayer, sacraments, and precautions; Satan is most dangerous when people think he is not around. Ordinary spiritual protection includes calling on the Lord for mercy, St. Michael the Archangel, St. Joseph as terror of demons, and the Blessed Mother. Ephesians 6 and the armor of God are referenced as teaching spiritual warfare.

The rosary is described as a gospel prayer centered on repeated Hail Marys while meditating on mysteries in the lives of Jesus and Mary. The repetition and physical beads are framed as aids to staying focused and drawing closer to Christ, not as magical objects. The rosary is presented as given by Our Lady to St. Dominic and as a way to draw near to Jesus through Mary's intercession. Traditionally there were 15 rosary mysteries: joyful, sorrowful, and glorious; Pope St. John Paul II added five luminous mysteries.

Our Lady of Guadalupe is presented as a powerful apparition tied to millions of conversions to Christ. The Guadalupe image is described as miraculously preserved on St. Juan Diego's cactus-cloth garment and still housed in the Basilica in Mexico City. Our Lady of Guadalupe appeared to Native American Juan Diego in 1531, from December 9th to the 12th. The image is described as showing the woman of the apocalypse: clothed with the sun, moon under her feet, stars over her head. Roses reportedly bloomed in winter on a craggy hill as a sign for the bishop; when Juan Diego opened his mantle, flowers fell out and the image appeared. The cactus-cloth garment is said to have should have disintegrated within 30 or 40 years but remains preserved.

A shrine to Our Lady of Guadalupe was founded in La Crosse, Wisconsin, with a five-year preparation reflecting on mysteries of Mary's life. The five-year preparation themes named are the Immaculate Conception, Perpetual Virginity, Divine Maternity, Assumption, and Mediation of All Graces. A five-year preparation is underway for the 500th anniversary of the Guadalupe apparition in 2031.

Job hunting now means an AI writes your résumé, an AI ranks it, and sometimes an AI interviews you at midnight. Greenhouse data says the average opening pulls hundreds of applications and about a 0.4% shot at the job.

Companies that still need a human answer are dragging candidates into the office for days. Foxglove even tells trialists to bring their favorite AI tools.

Business Insider writes that Foxglove now uses work trials for every role. Candidates ask if they can use AI. Ellis Neder, Foxglove's head of design: "We expect you to use AI, and we will give you whatever AI tools you want."

A work trial means doing real job tasks for days before an offer. An ATS is the software that ranks résumés before a human sees them. Congestion means so many applications that matching breaks.

A separate Business Insider look at Greenhouse data from last quarter puts the average opening at 242 applications, nearly triple 2017 at comparable unemployment, with an implied about 0.4% chance of getting the job. Greenhouse survey: 74% of candidates use AI in their job search. CEO Daniel Chait: "Nobody's happy with the current situation… Something broke in the technology."

Brookings analysis via BI: job postings requiring AI skills quadrupled from about 50,000 in March 2024 to nearly 200,000 last month. Stanford HAI: 90% of U.S. employers use AI screening.

In a study of 3.4 million people and 4 million applications, 26% of Black and 15% of Asian applicants hit positions where the AI showed adverse impact under the EEOC four-fifths rule, the federal fairness test for hiring screens.

AI on both sides of the gate. Then a week in the office.

There will be a lot of emotional answers to this because in practice it describes an opaque ingroup of influential and high-earning men in tech, and so credible accusations of sexual misconduct and fraud are par for the course and often someone’s introduction to the group.

Around 2010 in reaction to rampant fraud in NGOs and CA nonprofits, charity navigators like GiveWell and eventually OpenPhilanthropy became increasingly popular among young men in tech and policy looking to dip their toes in noblesse oblige. 

  As charity selection became increasingly dogmatic, those especially interested in scoping the marginal impact of a dollar, particularly those from financial backgrounds, began organizing under the term Effective Altruism (EA), and fundraised with very few scruples, whether that money came from child molesters or scam artists attempting to rehabilitate their public images. 

EA wasn’t limited to charity and fundraising though and took their Benthamite perspectives to futurism and transhumanism, forming something of a faith around the idea of alien superintelligence, or an artificial conscious mind unrecognizable as human in its capabilities or wants. 

Since the rank and file often self-select into big tech, EA offered them a heliocentric perspective where they, uniquely-equipped with LessWrong forum posts and bachelors from Stanford in CS, could herald in this modern, wrathful God so long as they clung tightly to the reins and dick-measured over who p(ortended) doom the most. 

As for why I don’t trust EA, it’s because they can’t self-govern themselves. They will run cover for anyone who gives them money, anyone who gives them 15 minutes of fame or credibility. text:
The Boy Who Learned to Write in Sand, and Opened the Door to Machines That Understand Human Speech....

No Electricity / Paper / Shoes Until His Teens. 

He Still Became the 1st Person of Asian Origin to Win the "Nobel Prize of Computing."

Every time we say Hey Siri / Alexa, play something / OK Google, a machine listens to our voice, breaks it into sound, and turns it into meaning. 

Those specific products sit on decades of later work, statistical models, deep neural networks, oceans of data, and product engineering at Apple, Amazon, and Google. 

But the idea that a computer could be taught to actually understand continuous human speech, not just recognize a handful of preset commands, and the 1st working research systems that proved it, that lineage opens with 1 man: a farmer's son from a small village in Andhra Pradesh.

His name is Dabbala Rajagopal Reddy. The world calls him Raj Reddy. 🙏🙏

As a child in the 1940s, Reddy grew up in rural Katur, in Chittoor district, Andhra Pradesh, a home with no electricity and no running water.

His 1 room schoolhouse had no paper / pencils, so the children learned to write their letters by tracing them into a plot of sand.

On hot nights, he and his 6 siblings would drag their mattresses outside just to sleep under a clear, star-filled sky.

He was the 1st person in his entire family to receive a college education. He has said he went barefoot through much of his childhood, and did not have a proper pair of shoes or sandals until he was around 16.

On the advice of an astrologer, his father, a farmer and landowner in the village, by his own account likely the most well off family among ~500 people there, though still poor by urban standards, sent him to study, with tuition itself paid for by an uncle.

Reddy went on to earn a Bachelor's degree in civil engineering from Guindy College of Engineering in Madras in 1958, then a Master's in Australia, before working briefly for IBM.

None of that path pointed toward AI. Not yet.

In 1963, Reddy arrived at Stanford University as a PhD student studying under 1 of the founding legends of AI himself, John McCarthy, the man who coined the very term "artificial intelligence."

Reddy went on to pioneer the construction of systems capable of recognizing continuous speech, developing one of the 1st such systems, called Hearsay I, and later refining the ideas through follow-on systems named Hearsay II and Harpy.

He and his students, through this body of work, developed many of the foundational ideas that the field of commercial speech recognition would later build on, including the blackboard model, a way of coordinating multiple sources of knowledge inside a single AI system, an idea that went on to be adopted across the wider field of applied AI.

1 of his own students, Jim Baker, later co-founded Dragon Systems with his wife Janet, a company built on the statistical approach to speech recognition that grew directly out of this research lineage, and that the whole industry would eventually adopt.

Think about the distance being covered here. A boy who once traced letters in sand because his classroom had no paper had, within a couple of decades, become one of the people teaching computers how to make sense of the human voice.

Reddy went on to found and lead the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon University, a place so closely tied to his name and presence that people at CMU affectionately nicknamed it the "Raj Mahal."

In 1994, Reddy and fellow AI researcher Edward Feigenbaum jointly won the ACM Turing Award, an honour so significant within computer science that it is routinely described as the field's equivalent of the Nobel Prize.

Reddy became the very first person of Asian origin in history to receive it. 🙏🙏

In his home state of India, he helped found the Rajiv Gandhi University of Knowledge Technologies, an institution built specifically to serve rural youth, the same population he himself had once come from.

At the RAISE 2020 summit, he pushed the argument that India needed to focus AI squarely on the ~400M people at the bottom of the economic pyramid, using speech recognition and translation technology to offer basic reading and learning capability to those who had never had access to it.

At a 2021 Computer History Museum event honouring his life's work, he reminded the audience, in his own words, that half the world still does not benefit from the technologies people like him have spent careers building.

Bharat itself eventually recognised him with the Padma Bhushan in 2001. But ask most Indians, including plenty who use voice assistants on their phones every single day, who Raj Reddy is, and you will very likely get silence.
